headline: Tax changes are pulling investors out of property, but the asset remains investable with more selective stock-picking; ongoing supply constraints and rental market pressure will continue to support the market
reasoning: Rob Gilmour acknowledges that much of the current price weakness is driven by investors exiting the market, which aligns with the government's tax policy objectives, while the impact on owner-occupiers has been more limited. He argues this does not make property uninvestable but rather demands a more discerning approach. He stresses the need to encourage investment in rental properties to keep rents stable and support new construction to address the supply deficit, with the supply constraint likely to remain a structural support for the market.
quote: I think well, we've seen a big part of the decline is investors pulling out of the market and that's definitely part of the objective of the tax changes and the impact on owner occupies a lot less. And I and I think it does, you know, create a better lens to assess how you invest in property. But I don't think it makes property an uninvestable asset. I think you need to be more, more choosy. And ultimately we do need to encourage investment into the property market. headline: Supply-demand shortfall and rising construction costs provide a structural floor under Australian housing; improving yields in some markets now look attractive relative to the RBA cash rate
reasoning: Rob Gilmour notes that land scarcity and the fact that construction costs never decline create a natural price floor for well-located Australian residential property. He cautions against buying in areas with large development pipelines due to elevated supply and tenant competition, but argues that as rents rise and prices soften, yields are improving to the point where they compare favourably to the RBA cash rate in some markets. This improving yield dynamic should eventually bring buyers and sellers together.
quote: Look, it definitely does. I mean, you hear, you know, property investing, you know, the land is scarce, construction costs never go down. That naturally does put a floor where you've got a location that's always in demand and the cost to build is always there... the cost to build a property is definitely not getting cheaper and that is going to ultimately put a floor on the market. But what investors will also be looking at is, you know, the yield that they'll be getting. And so buyer will need to meet seller and, and we're starting to see when the rents are going up and the prices are coming down, that yield is going up. headline: SMSF sector booming with ~50,000 new funds last financial year, driven by a younger 25-44 cohort seeking control and broader investment access, but long-term engagement risk is a concern
reasoning: Gilmour highlights that the SMSF sector is showing strong momentum with approximately 50,000 new funds established in the last financial year, with the growth skewing toward younger members aged 25-44 — a demographic shift from the historically older SMSF base (85% of current owners are over 45). He attributes this to greater financial literacy, easy online setup, and the desire for more control and investment choice. However, he flags the risk that younger members may lose engagement over time and fail to make proactive long-term investment decisions, questioning whether the structure is appropriate for everyone.
quote: The data that's come out recently shows that the SMSF sector is really, really strong. There were about 50,000 new funds that were created last financial year. So there's a lot of a lot of momentum with people wanting to set up an SMSF. And interestingly, that's coming from a younger cohort. So most of those new establishments are coming in the age group between 25 and 44... I do wonder what that will look like if they happen to lose engagement along the way and actually not be proactive with making those important long term investment decisions.

headline: Government's discretionary trust 'fixed entitlement' olive branch is legally risky for trustees and practically unworkable — treat with high caution
reasoning: Gilmour warns that the government's proposed concession allowing trustees to permanently fix beneficiary entitlements to avoid the 30% tax is fraught with legal exposure. A trustee of a discretionary trust owes duties to a broad range of potential beneficiaries, and making a fixed decision favouring a limited subset could leave the trustee legally liable for not considering all beneficiaries' interests. He views the option as moving too far toward a fixed trust structure and not practically workable, recommending it be treated with a high degree of caution.
quote: If you're a trustee of a discretionary trust, you have a very broad range of potential beneficiaries out there. And if you're making a decision to actually make a fixed decision on, on a limited subset of those beneficiaries, then you as a trustee can be legally exposed to making that decision because you're not taking into account the interests of all of your trustees. So it's something to be considered very, very carefully if you're looking down that option. And in my view, it's not really workable because of risks like that.

headline: Rate hikes favour patience on equity deployment; floating-rate fixed interest still a good parking spot but stretched equity valuations are a concern
reasoning: Rob Gilmour notes that while rate rises benefit retirees and cash savers, the global trend of rising interest rates is putting pressure on equity markets where valuations look stretched. He suggests investors can afford to be more patient with investment decisions and that floating-rate fixed interest investments remain a sound place to park money in the current environment.
quote: I think it does have ramifications when it comes to investment decisions. Obviously you're getting paid more for cash in the bank. So being a little bit more patient with regards to investment decisions, you're you can afford to take a bit more time floating rate fixed interest investments still a very good place to park money. But where the concern is, is that there is a global trend with interest rates going going up and that is going to ultimately put pressure on equity markets where some of those valuations are, are looking pretty stretched.
